1:#!/usr/bin/env bash
2:# Print a rung's briefing, or any slice of the record (FACTS.md, INDEX.md, POSITIONS.md, the ledger, the maps, a note by heading); --help for the usage.

usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  F-87, P-48             the entry of that number in FACTS.md or POSITIONS.md
  F-87+                  the entry, then each entry it points to and each entry
                         that points to it, each once, one level
  history:F-87           the entry's blocks in FACTS-history.md or
                         POSITIONS-history.md, oldest first: the provenance line
                         of each change and the line it replaced
  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's
                         title is its bold opening, or where it has none, its
                         opening words up to the first colon, semicolon or full
                         stop; when no current title holds it, the entry one of
                         whose former titles (in FACTS-history.md) does, with a
                         line saying it was retitled
  section:HEADING        every entry of the FACTS.md section whose heading holds HEADING
  index:WORDS            the INDEX.md lines that hold every one of WORDS (at most 10)
  ledger:ROW             row ROW of the gap ledger, whole, under its section and
                         the table's header
  ledger-find:WORDS      one line for each gap ledger row that holds every one of
                         WORDS: its number, its status and the first 150 characters
                         of its claim (at most 10, then how many more matched)
  positions:TITLE        the entry of POSITIONS.md whose bold title holds TITLE, as
                         a TITLE query does in FACTS.md, former titles included;
                         exactly one must, else the nearest titles are named
  positions:DATE WORDS   the entry of POSITIONS.md dated DATE (YYYY-MM-DD, the first
                         date in the entry) whose head, the entry's text up to its
                         first colon and space, holds every one of WORDS; when no
                         entry of POSITIONS.md matches, the entry of
                         POSITIONS-history.md, from the latest of its sections
                         that hold one, with the line saying what became of
                         it; the output says which file it came from
  map:FILE#HEADING       the section of explorations/coordinator/map/FILE whose
                         heading holds HEADING, down to the next heading of its level
  doc:PATH#HEADING       the same for any note, PATH from the repository root, such
                         as a judge's ruling; doc:PATH alone prints the whole note;
                         in a .tex or .tick file the headings are its \chapter, \section,
                         \subsection, \subsubsection and \paragraph titles,
                         matched with their macros dropped; a heading equal to
                         HEADING wins over the headings that merely hold it, and
                         HEADING may be a path, A > B, for B's section inside A's
  map:FILE#HEADING@WORDS, doc:PATH#HEADING@WORDS
                         only the table rows and list items of that section that
                         hold every one of WORDS, a row under its table's header,
                         and the paragraphs whose bold lead holds them
  code:PATH#FROM         the declaration that starts on the one line of PATH that
                         holds FROM, with its line numbers: in .java, .scala and
                         .js through the brace that closes it, elsewhere (.fss,
                         .fsi) through its more indented lines and its end
  code:PATH#FROM..TO     from the declaration at FROM through the end of the
                         one at the first line after it that holds TO
WORDS match as whole words, or as the start of one when a word ends in *.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:96
- P-165 **`asFloat` and the `=` built on it leave `trait Number`; each built-in number type keeps its own `asFloat`.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32`, `RR64` and `IntLiteral` each declare `asFloat`, so the written conversion `asFloat(x)` into `RR64` is unchanged at every concrete type. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other (P-74); otherwise the program writes the conversion, `asFloat(x) = y`. The vector norm takes a bound that promises a float; its form is the default of a fork on his review list: the norm at each of the eight number types, each by its own `asFloat` (F-324). `Float`'s `^` at a `Number` exponent, `random`, `atan2` and `printThreadInfo` are declared at `RR64`, and coercion carries `ZZ32`, `RR32` and numerals to them. The specification's sentence follows (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:46-54`). P-74's rule, an exact conversion implicit and a lossy one written, stands. Why: the team's compiler prelude declares `Number` with nothing in it (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:510`), and the specification does not ground the method: its sentence that names it on `Number` is the revival's revision. The curator's rule for such a case: an early idea of the interpreter's library goes where the specification does not ground it and the later prelude eliminated it. With `Number` open (P-160), an abstract `asFloat` would force a program's own number, such as a complex number, to invent a float, and `Number`'s `=` would compare two different complex numbers by it.

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## Landed semantics

FACTS.md:232
- F-324 **The one library's `Number` declares nothing; each number type declares its own `asFloat` and an `=` at each type it coerces from or into.** It builds P-160's second step and P-165. `Number`'s `comprises` clause, `asFloat`, `=` and `exactValue` are struck (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:380-381`, `.fsi:288-289`); the nine types declare `asFloat` in their apis; 42 declarations give a pair of `=` for each of the 21 coercions, so two numbers of different types compare by value where a coercion joins them, and otherwise by the fallback `a SEQV b` or a written `asFloat(x) = y`; the vector norm is declared at each of the eight types; the reflective generator chooses among the five former listed types. A program's own number type compares by its own `=` or by the fallback. Gated by `tests/NumberOwnTypeNoAsFloatWalk`, `NumberEqualityOwnTypeWalk`, `NumberMixedEqualityWalk`, `VectorNormElementTypesWalk`, `NumberOwnTypeArrayWalk`, `NumberOpenTraitPlusBesideArrayWalk` and the team's `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-number-open/REPORT.md`.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:70
- P-160 **The one library's `Number` opens: its `comprises` clause goes, so that a program may declare its own number type below `Number`.** The team's compiler prelude, the specification and the team's test `tests/extendNumber.fss` give `Number` no such clause. ### A small test to preserve through consolidation

Keep the quiz and audit as historical evidence. Select a small set of consequential wrong assumptions from them and actual worker failures, then update the expected answers against the current record. The October 8 audit itself contains statements that later work may have changed; do not use its old answers as a timeless oracle.

For the whole-Revival consolidation, give a fresh reader the core skill, the proposed whole orientation and neutral task questions, without the audit or answer key. Grade concrete choices, including the path and scope qualifications, rather than its ability to repeat headings. For example: how to run a source program; what to do when the specification and an implementation disagree; and whether a numeric relationship or conversion assumed from another language holds here. Include a case where the right action is to follow a task-specific pointer or explore, not invent an answer.

The reviewer has the expected answers and evidence. Record missed corrections and new false assumptions. Compare old and new skill versions on the same cases when judging a consolidation regression. For later small edits, rerun only the affected cases; refresh the pretraining-only baseline when a materially different worker model makes that useful. This is a proposed bounded regression practice, not a claim that the earlier experiment already implemented it.

== explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md:252-260

### Operationalize the admission test, not another writing ritual

For consolidation, apply the admission test to each candidate correction. For later landings, apply it to each proposed addition or substantive edit. An established trap can reuse its evidence; do not rerun a baseline merely to satisfy a form. When necessity is uncertain, use a fresh-reader test.

A small Claude Workflow could separate three jobs: a scenario author establishes the expected decision and its evidence; fresh readers answer neutral matched scenarios with and without the candidate correction; a grader compares answers against the evidence. For an incremental edit, the baseline should normally be the existing skill **without the candidate**, not an entirely unassisted worker. Otherwise the test cannot show that this particular addition is needed. A no-skill baseline remains useful for discovering broader pretraining assumptions.

The scenario author and grader may see the record; test readers must not see the expected answers or each other's responses. Require correct decisions and scope, not recitation. A candidate earns space when it addresses an evidenced wrong assumption or consequential missing knowledge; if the baseline already handles the case, seek evidence from other relevant failures before retaining it. One passing answer is not proof that every future worker will know it.

This is a workflow outline for Claude to reconcile with the recovered run, not a claim about how that run was implemented. Keep the writer's instruction small: **identify the mistaken assumption, show why it is expected, and verify that the correction prevents the mistake without introducing another.** Preserve evaluation evidence in maintenance records. No skill files or workflow code were changed in this review.

# What the revival changed in the team's Fortress

This part gives the departures of revived Fortress from the team's Fortress, and from what you expect from Java, Scala, Haskell or Julia. The team left three forms that disagree: the specification, walk with the interpreter's library, and the compiled path with the compiler's library. The rules below resolve them. Read the part whole, after `SKILL.md`, before work.

Each bold rule states the rule of this tree. A sentence that names a POSITIONS entry (P-N) states a decision of the curator. Build on a sentence without one, but do not cite it as a decision. Question a rule only on new evidence (`SKILL.md`, "When to explore"). Most rules follow the team's later type papers (`Papers/`) over the specification's early text (P-26; `exploring.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. Where a rule changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`).

A sentence that cites a ledger row states a known departure of one path from a bold rule. A fix can change it, so do not assert it as correct in a test. A sentence that opens "Until the switch-over" states a limit of the compiler's library. The limit ends when the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, so do not fix it in the compiler's prelude (`compiler.md`). If a change is not here, search FACTS and POSITIONS (`records.md`) before you call a disagreement a conflict. An old note, a team test and your training can be right about the team's walk and wrong here: the number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, and walk converts arguments.

## Dispatch and overloading

**Overloads may differ in their static parameters (P-45).** An example is `ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T` beside `ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T`. The Working Draft forbids such pairs. A declaration's declared domain is the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept at some instance within its bounds: every `Shape` for the first `ident`. The checker applies the overloading rules of `SKILL.md` to declared domains. The more specific declaration's return type must be a subtype of the other's at every instance, not at one only.

**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value of both domains has one instance of each generic type at each position, so those instances' static arguments are equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair where the equalities leave a static parameter free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.

**Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations.** It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".

**Walk's load check is not the verdict of these rules.** It refuses some valid pairs and loads some invalid ones, and the checker differs from it on others. Before you change code to pass walk's check, or take its acceptance as proof, find the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks": a case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk. For example, walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains only at a call (row 780).

**Two functional methods with equivalent parameter types are duplicates, wherever `self` stands.** So the checker refuses `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` in a trait `S`. Abstract declarations count:

- both paths refuse an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one trait;
- both paths refuse an object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another, unless the object declares the method itself (P-149). The Scala language accepts it.

The Meet Rule asks for a declaration that covers the meet of two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest (`SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language"). An abstract functional method also counts for it. So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`. Likewise, a program's trait that declares its own functional `+` overlaps the library's `+` between an array and a number, because `Number` is open (P-160). Declare the trait `excludes { Number }`, or make it exclude arrays. Otherwise walk refuses the program at load: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker refuses such a pair in one component, but accepts it against the library's `+` (row 918). The library's `-`, `MIN` and `MAX` have the same form, but only `+` was measured.

## Traits and objects

**The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97).** It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk does not apply the rule: it runs such a type, and refuses overloads on two instantiations, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, because it does not read them as excluding (row 416). The specification marks the Working Draft's examples that break the rule "Not allowed": do not copy them.

**A `comprises` clause speaks of values (P-60).** Every value of the trait that declares it is a value of a listed type. So a generic trait need not be listed if every type below it is below a listed type, as `Integral[\I\]` below `AnyIntegral`. A Java `permits` list names each direct subtype; this clause need not. Read so, several declarations can together cover the meet of two overloads. At load, walk checks extenders only against the clauses of the program's main component (row 551).

**`override` widens.** An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than its own. To replace an inherited declaration at its own parameter types, declare it again without `override`. An `override` in a trait also overrides in every type below it. The checker checks that an overriding return type is a subtype. Walk refuses at load an `override` that, by this rule, overrides nothing, so a Java-style `override` in the library stops every program. Two departures: the checker accepts such an `override` (row 653), and the code generator refuses every `override` modifier (row 650).

**An object defines an inherited abstract method by bodies that together cover its parameter types (P-147).** It needs one body at those types, or several narrower bodies that cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk refuses at load an object without static parameters that leaves one uncovered. Walk skips this check for a generic object (row 665). Walk stops its search for a cover at limits that `interpreter.md` gives, and the checker at the same limits. The checker refuses a cover by several bodies where the abstract or a covering method has static parameters (row 725).

**In a self-typed trait the checker types `self` as the trait met with the implementing type.** A trait `T` is self-typed if both conditions hold:

- `T` has no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`;
- `T` has a parameter `X` bounded by `T` itself, as `trait T[\X extends T[\X\]\]` (P-146), or by a self-typed trait `U[\X\]` that `T` extends, as `trait T[\X extends U[\X\]\] extends U[\X\]`.

Walk reads `self` in the same way, so it loads such a pair in the library and in a program's own component. A function over `Index` and one over a tuple of `Index` types do not exclude each other. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `Index`, so a program that names it does not compile. Two departures:

- the checker refuses a tuple expression at a parameter of type `Index`, but takes one at a parameter of type `I`, where `I extends Index` (row 805);
- walk loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it (row 806).

**Pairs and triples are ordered only where each element type extends `StandardPartialOrder`.** This holds for `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP`. Walk refuses another element type at the call, also where earlier elements decide, as `(1,()) < (2,())`. It also refuses numbers of two run-time types at one position, as `(1,2) < (1,2.5)` (row 511). Unordered deciding elements give `false`, or `Unordered` for `CMP`. The checker orders a `List[\E\]` only where `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]`, so a list of `RR64` has no order there (P-154). Walk orders every list (row 774). A list's `=` stays element by element.

**Where a type declares no `=`, `=` is strict equivalence, `SEQV` (P-168).** The library's `=` over `Any` answers `a SEQV b`. `SEQV` follows the specification on both paths:

- values of different types are never equivalent;
- a value object is equivalent field by field, a tuple element by element, and a float by its bits;

So a value object without its own `=` that holds a string is not `=` to an equal one built apart. Nor is a tuple of four or more elements, because the library declares `=` on pairs and triples only (row 923). A type's own `=` decides wherever the type declares one, and a string's `=` compares text. Give the value object an `=`, or compare the parts. `tests-writing.md` gives how `assert` reaches a type's `=`. Until the switch-over, a compiled `===` reaches the prelude's operators, which compare strings and the four number types by `=` (row 908).

**A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, not Scala's `Nothing` (P-48).** The checker takes the intersection of its upper bounds, narrowed by the expected type. - one that an argument bounds only from above, with a bound that names another static parameter (row 612);

Such a call does not run compiled yet. Until the switch-over, compiled programs do not link `NatReflect`, which is part of the interpreter's library. After the switch-over, such a call still fails, for a second reason. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, so its `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size. A compiled call fails the JVM's verification if it passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected (row 307). This holds for a program's own trait too.

## Numbers

**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** The record calls this choice route A. Route C is the way not chosen: a checker rule under which the number types could nest again. The record still calls the number and order traits "the tower". That word does not mean that they nest.

**Under walk a numeral has a run-time class.** The checker types an integer numeral as `IntLiteral`, a sibling under `Number` that converts to the integer types, `QQ` and `RR64` (P-76). Walk gives a numeral the class `Int`, `Long` or `BigNum` by its value. These classes stand for `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ`, but a generic instantiates at the class. Walk prints these classes by the traits' names, also inside static arguments, so a printed type does not show the instance: `Cell(3)` prints `Cell[\ZZ32\]` but is a `Cell[\Int\]` (row 364). Walk's own error messages still say `Int`. Walk answers `IntLiteral`'s arithmetic as a `ZZ32` (row 578). The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or `Matrix` only at the eight number types, not at a user subtype of `Number`. Elsewhere they give a plain array, whose `+` and unary `-` fail dispatch under walk. Under walk, an inferred element type is a run-time class, so they give a plain array (row 721). Write the static argument.

**Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". Where the tied declarations differ only at the positions of the call's numerals, the checker reads the numeral as `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where the value does not fit.

**`Number` declares nothing (P-165).** Each of the eight number types, and `IntLiteral`, declares its own `asFloat` into `RR64`. So generic code over `T extends Number` can call nothing on a `T`, not even `asFloat`. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error: `1/2 = 0.5` is `false`, as is a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. To compare values across types, write `asFloat(x) = y`. A program may declare its own number type below `Number`, which has no `comprises` clause (P-160).

**An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).

**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. Convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.

## Reductions and comprehensions

A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.

**A reduction's static argument depends on the path.** The checker does not infer it for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, whose bound names the parameter (row 731). Write it in every clause form, as `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Other reductions take their bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types. If that join is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1". Departures under walk:

- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (rows 20, 717);
- a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).

**A reduction without an identity lifts its elements to `Maybe[\R\]` inside the reduction.** `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and the string reduction `BIG //` extend `AssociativeReduction[\R\]`, whose `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`. `BIG MAX` over a generator still answers `R`. Walk refuses at load a reduction without static parameters that declares `simpleJoin` at `Any` or untyped. A generic one stops at its first join. The team's tests declare `simpleJoin` so: do not copy them.

## Implementation limits

**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). So walk runs programs that the checker refuses. Besides a `Boolean`, it takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. It refuses any other value. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition. The compiled path's own limits are in `compiler.md`.

**Write every parameter type.** The compiled path refuses a parameter without a type, of a function, a method or a local function: "Missing parameter type for". Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types. With none or several, the checker types the body.

component NumberOpenTraitPlusBesideArrayWalk
export Executable

(*) Under walk, a program's trait that excludes neither Number nor arrays and declares its own functional + is refused at load beside the library's + between an array and a number, now that Number is open.

trait Wide excludes { String }
  getter big(): ZZ32
  opr +(self, other: Wide): Wide = WideOf(self.big + other.big)
end
object WideOf(b: ZZ32) extends Wide
  getter big(): ZZ32 = b
end

run(): () = do
    assert((WideOf(1) + WideOf(2)).big, 3, "a program's trait's own + runs where walk loads it")
  end

end
load_exception_contains=fails the Meet Rule: neither is found to be more specific than the other or to exclude it
----
component ExclusionVectorScalarWalk
export Executable

(* Operators on an array of a number type and a number, on either side, beside the additive group's own operator are a valid overloading where a vector is both an array and an additive group, since no value is both an array and a number, and each call runs the declaration its arguments select (traits.tex, section "Trait Declarations"; overloading.tex, sections "Incompatibility Rule" and "Declarations with Static Parameters"). *)

trait AnyAddG end
trait AddG[\T extends AddG[\T\]\] extends AnyAddG
    opr PLUS(self, other: T): String
end
trait Numb end
trait HasRk excludes { Numb } end
object Rr extends { Numb, AddG[\Rr\] }
    opr PLUS(self, other: Rr): String = "number"
end
trait Arry[\E\] extends HasRk end
object Vv extends { Arry[\Rr\], AddG[\Vv\] }
    opr PLUS(self, other: Vv): String = "vector"
end

opr PLUS[\T extends { Numb, AddG[\T\] }\](x: Arry[\T\], y: T): String = "array and number"
opr PLUS[\T extends { Numb, AddG[\T\] }\](y: T, x: Arry[\T\]): String = "number and array"

run(): () = do
    assert(Rr PLUS Rr, "number", "two numbers run the number's own operator")
    assert(Vv PLUS Vv, "vector", "two vectors run the vector's own operator")
    assert(Vv PLUS Rr, "array and number", "a vector and a number run the array's operator")
    assert(Rr PLUS Vv, "number and array", "a number and a vector run the array's operator")
    println("PASS")
  end

end
